slides.title: Two views of one signal
slides.narration: A periodic signal can be viewed in time, as a waveform, or in frequency, as a collection of sinusoidal ingredients.

slides.title: The periodic square wave
slides.caption: x(t)=\begin{cases}A,&0<t<T/2\\-A,&T/2<t<T\end{cases},\qquad x(t+T)=x(t)
slides.narration: Start with a square wave of amplitude A. It stays high for half a period, low for half a period, and then repeats.

slides.title: Finding the fundamental
slides.caption: \omega=\frac{2\pi}{T}
slides.narration: A period T corresponds to a fundamental angular frequency of two pi over T. This is the first location in the spectrum.

slides.title: The first harmonic
slides.caption: x_1(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\sin(\omega t)
slides.narration: The fundamental sinusoid gives the broad shape of the square wave. Its frequency is omega, and its spectral amplitude is 4A over pi.

slides.title: Adding the third harmonic
slides.caption: x_3(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}\right)
slides.narration: Now add a sinusoid three times as fast, but only one third as strong. Their sum begins to look much more like a square wave.

slides.title: More odd harmonics
slides.caption: x_7(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}+\frac{\sin(5\omega t)}{5}+\frac{\sin(7\omega t)}{7}\right)
slides.narration: The fifth and seventh harmonics sharpen the transitions further. Each new harmonic is faster and weaker than the previous one.

slides.title: The finite approximation
slides.caption: S_N(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\sum_{m=0}^{N}\frac{\sin\big((2m+1)\omega t\big)}{2m+1}
slides.narration: All of these partial sums follow one rule: include the first N plus one odd harmonics, each divided by its odd harmonic number.

slides.title: A term becomes a spike
slides.caption: \text{frequency of term }m=(2m+1)\omega,\qquad \text{amplitude of term }m=\frac{4A}{\pi(2m+1)}
slides.narration: Every sinusoid leaves one spike in the spectrum. The spike position records its frequency, and its height records its amplitude.

slides.title: The limiting reconstruction
slides.caption: x(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin(\omega t)+\frac{\sin(3\omega t)}{3}+\frac{\sin(5\omega t)}{5}+\cdots\right)
slides.narration: As more odd harmonics are added, the partial sum approaches the square wave wherever the wave is continuous. At a jump, it converges to zero, while the Gibbs overshoot remains visible nearby.

slides.title: Fourier reconstruction in 3D
slides.caption: z(t,N)=\frac{4A}{\pi}\sum_{m=0}^{3}\frac{e^{-(2m+1)N}\sin((2m+1)\omega t)}{2m+1},\qquad N\geq0
slides.bridge: so the harmonic sum becomes a surface
slides.narration: The centered square wave is reconstructed by adding its odd sinusoidal harmonics. The frequencies are omega, 3 omega, 5 omega, and so on, and their amplitudes decrease in proportion to 1, one third, one fifth, and so on.
